The valley's apartment complexes, one by one उपत्यकाका अपार्टमेन्टहरू

Nepal keeps no public register of its apartment buildings. A buyer who wants to know who built a tower, when, how tall it is, what happened to it in 2015 and what its flats ask today has to piece that together from old newspaper archives, developer brochures and listing sites. This page does the piecing for every complex we could find, and every claim in it links to the page it came from.

What the dossiers add up to

The market in the government's and the developers' own numbers

No official series exists. These are the counts the Department of Urban Development and the developers' association gave the press, in the order they gave them. They measure different things, and the differences matter. A project licensed is not a building built, and a building built is not a building lived in.

    The list of nineteen, November 2011

    The Department of Urban Development and Building Construction moved to stop ownership transfers in nineteen projects. Thirteen had taken bookings and started building without an environmental study or a structural permit, and six had not handed over their paperwork. Where they stand now:

    The inspections, May and June 2015

    After the Gorkha earthquake a government team put a sticker on every inhabited high-rise apartment building: red for unsafe, yellow for repair before living there, green for safe.

    Where every line comes from

    The starting list came from four places. The first was housingnepal.com's directory of housing projects, which gives a developer, a unit count and a start date for many of them. The second was the government's own November 2011 list of nineteen non-compliant projects. The third was the buildings inspected after the 2015 earthquake. The fourth was every apartment building named on OpenStreetMap or named in a nepalhomes.com listing. Each complex was then researched separately in English and Nepali sources: national newspapers, the business press, developer and contractor portfolios, the architects' own project pages and listing sites. A claim is in a dossier only if a source we opened says it. The few exceptions rest on a search result's own summary and are marked quoted from a search result. Each source is numbered under the claim it supports, with the supporting sentence quoted beside it.

    Where sources disagree, both versions are kept and listed under Where the sources disagree. Where a dossier is thin, it says what could not be found. Each one carries a confidence grade: high means several independent sources agree, low means one listing or one directory entry. The grade is about how well the facts are documented, not about the quality of the building.

    Prices are asking prices. Nepal publishes no transaction prices for flats. The current prices come from nepalhomes.com listings that the site itself ties to a named complex, captured on 17 September 2026. A listing whose tole contradicts its complex is dropped, so a "Sun City" flat advertised in Sanepa does not count. Older prices are quoted from news and brochures with their dates. Per square foot means built-up area as the seller states it. That figure usually includes a share of corridors and walls and is not comparable to carpet area.

    Locations. A marker is on the building itself where OpenStreetMap has it mapped by name. Otherwise it sits at the street or tole the sources name, and it is drawn hollow so it never looks more exact than it is.

    What is left out. Housing colonies of standalone houses, hotels, serviced apartments let to tourists, and single-owner buildings let floor by floor. Projects that were announced and never built stay in, marked as such, because a buyer who paid a deposit on one still needs to know about it.

    Looked at and left out

    Candidates that turned out to be houses, offices or another complex under a second name, or that nothing shows to be a developer-built complex at all. Each was researched like the rest, and this is what settled it.

      Research done October 2026. Buildings change hands, stall and restart. A dossier is a record of what was published, not a survey of the building today. Anyone deciding on a flat should still ask the owners' society for the completion certificate, the structural drawings and the lift and water records.
